slides.title: Pythagorean Theorem in Real-World Problems
slides.note: Post the learning target. Say one line and nothing else yet: “Today the triangle is hidden in a ladder, a ramp, a screen or a garden: find it first.”

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.note: Q4 is today's first move: every rectangle — a screen, a lawn, a box — has four right angles, so its diagonal is a hypotenuse. Say that after the reveal. Two minutes silent, then reveal.

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.note: Reveal. Ask for the band each question came from only if time allows.

slides.title: Vocabulary
slides.sub: The new words, before they are used.
slides.note: Read each word and its meaning once; the notes use them next. Students copy the words, not the definitions.

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
Before any number: where is the square corner? A wall meets the ground square, so a leaning ladder is c. A rectangle's corner is square, so a screen's or a lawn's diagonal is c. A ramp's rise stands square on the ground, so the ramp's surface is c. A kite's string runs from the ground to the kite above a point on the ground, so the string is c. Sketch it, mark the corner, name c — then the theorem.
OFF: 'Sketch it. Mark the square corner. Name c.'

slides.title: Notes
slides.sub: A garden 6 m by 8 m, and a path from corner to corner.
slides.note:
A garden 6 m by 8 m with a path from corner to corner. The garden's corner is square, so the path is c: 36 + 64 = 100 and the path is 10 m. Walking along two sides is 6 + 8 = 14 m, so the path is 4 m shorter — the question board 5 and the test ask.
OFF: 'A rectangle's diagonal is always a hypotenuse.'

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
A 10-ft ladder with its foot 3 ft from the wall: the ladder is c, so the height is a leg — subtract. 100 − 9 = 91, and the ladder reaches √91 ≈ 9.5 ft. The state guide's own item (B1G-M, MA.8.GR.1.1), worked here so no board repeats it.
OFF: 'How high is a leg. Subtract.'

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: Ask where the square corner is before any number: under the high end, where the rise meets the ground. So the ramp is c.

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: The rise and the run are the legs; the ramp is c. 4 + 169 = 173, √173 ≈ 13.15, so 13.2 ft — a little longer than the run, as a gentle ramp is. A board with 15 added the rise and the run.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: A screen's corner is square, so the diagonal is c: 49 + 100 = 149 and √149 ≈ 12.21, so 12.2 in — a board with 17 added the sides.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.title: Example 2
slides.note: Ask which length is c before anyone squares: the ladder, 8 ft. The height is a leg — so this one subtracts.

slides.title: Example 2
slides.note: The ladder is c: h² = 64 − 9 = 55, √55 ≈ 7.42, so 7.4 ft — less than 8, as a leg must be. A board with 8.5 added the squares (√73): an 8-ft ladder cannot reach 8.5 ft.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: 169 − 36 = 133 and √133 ≈ 11.53, so 11.5 ft — a board with 14.3 added the squares (√205), higher than the ladder is long.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.note: The pool's corner is square, so both sides are legs and the diagonal is c. A board with 17 added the sides; a board with 10.9 subtracted, 144 − 25, as if the 12 were c — here it is a side.
